name: Payment Networks
era: Modern form since BankAmericard (1958) → Visa (1970s); still dominant

chain.relation_note: Networks sit on the same money flow as banks: banks issue the cards and lend, the network moves the authorization and clips a toll. Neither works without the other.

suggested_next.why: Stripe, Adyen, Square — the layer merchants actually touch, sitting on top of the network rails.
The side that collects the fat interchange the network directs to it — the other half of the two-sided machine.
FedNow, account-to-account, and stablecoins aim to move money without the card toll — the modern threat to the rails.

one_line: Own the rails money rides on, clip a thin toll off every trip — and never touch the money itself.

engine.inputs: A tap or a swipe — a request to move money between a shopper's bank and a merchant's bank
engine.transformation: Route the authorization across the network, set the fee schedule, and guarantee the transaction settles
engine.outputs: A cleared payment, and a stream of tiny per-transaction fees
engine.money_in: Network assessment/service fees (~0.13–0.14% of volume), per-transaction data-processing fees, and premium cross-border fees
engine.money_out: Running the rails, fraud/security, incentives paid to banks to issue the network's cards
engine.the_spread: a tiny % of an enormous volume  (fee-per-swipe × trillions in flow)
engine.leverage_point: Asset-light: the network owns no cash and no receivables — it taxes movement, so revenue scales with total spend at near-zero marginal cost

unit.unit_economics: On a $100 US credit purchase the merchant loses ~$2–3 total. Almost all of that (~86% of the merchant's cost) is interchange that goes to the shopper's BANK, not the network. The network itself keeps only its thin assessment (~$0.13–0.14) plus small data-processing fees. Figures ballpark; vary by card type and geography.
unit.what_one_unit_produces: Data on the transaction, one more reason every merchant must accept the network, and one more reason every bank wants to issue its cards — the flywheel tightening by one turn.

plays.tagline: Don't hold the money. Tax the movement.

flow.step_desc: Own the rails every card payment must cross.
Take a fraction of a percent of each transaction — too small to fight, on every purchase.
Revenue rises with total volume at almost no extra cost, because you own no balance sheet.

plays.the_move: A tiny toll is invisible per-swipe and colossal across trillions. Own the road, not the cars.
plays.in_the_wild: In fiscal 2025 Visa processed roughly $14 trillion in payments volume across ~258 billion transactions and reported about $40 billion in net revenue; Mastercard handled around $9.2 trillion in gross dollar volume.
plays.watch_out: The toll is a regulatory target. Caps and antitrust settlements can compress the take rate you rely on.

plays.tagline: Route the fat fee to the banks so they push your card.

flow.step_desc: The network SETS the ~2% interchange fee — but doesn't keep it.
That fat fee flows to the bank that issued the shopper's card.
Rich interchange makes every issuer want to hand out YOUR cards, not a rival's.

plays.the_move: Give away the big fee to align the banks; keep the small, unstoppable one for yourself.
plays.in_the_wild: Interchange makes up the large majority of the merchant's swipe cost — combined US credit interchange averaged about 2.36% in 2025 — and it funds the rewards programs banks use to compete for cardholders.
plays.watch_out: This is what regulators attack: the US Durbin Amendment capped debit interchange, gutting that slice for issuers overnight.

plays.tagline: The fattest margin lives at the border.

flow.step_desc: A cardholder pays outside their home country.
Cross-border and currency-conversion fees apply on top of the normal toll.
These are among the network's most profitable transactions.

plays.the_move: Same rails, higher toll — charge a premium exactly where travelers have no alternative.
plays.in_the_wild: Cross-border is a disproportionately profitable line for both Visa and Mastercard, though its volume growth has decelerated for three straight years into 2025.
plays.watch_out: Cross-border volume tracks travel and trade — it slumps in downturns and pandemics, taking the premium with it.

plays.tagline: Every cardholder pulls a merchant; every merchant pulls a cardholder.

flow.step_desc: Get cards into wallets AND terminals into stores.
A merchant can't decline the network everyone carries; a shopper wants the card accepted everywhere.
Each new cardholder makes acceptance more essential, and vice versa — a self-tightening loop.

plays.the_move: Don't out-feature rivals — out-network them. Ubiquity itself becomes the product no one can copy.
plays.in_the_wild: Visa and Mastercard together account for more than 80% of US credit card transaction volume; challengers struggle to break a moat built on universal acceptance.
plays.watch_out: The same ubiquity draws antitrust scrutiny — and new rails can bootstrap their own network effect from a big platform's user base.

plays.tagline: Once you own the rails, sell services on top of them.

flow.step_desc: The core transaction fee funds everything.
Fraud scoring, tokenization, data analytics, consulting, real-time-payment products.
Value-added services grow faster than the toll and hedge against interchange pressure.

plays.the_move: Turn the rails into a platform — sell the tools everyone riding them needs.
plays.in_the_wild: Both networks have pushed hard into value-added services and acquisitions to grow revenue beyond pure transaction fees as regulatory pressure on interchange rises.
plays.watch_out: Services revenue is more competitive and less moat-protected than the toll — it's a real market, not a tollgate.

mechanics_summary.note: Sit on a flow and charge a small fee each time value passes — the purest version of this mechanic.
Cardholders and merchants each make the other side more valuable; the loop is the moat.
The network owns no money and no credit risk — it taxes movement, so it scales almost for free.
Take a cut of transactions you host without being party to them.
Route the fat interchange to banks so issuance (your complement) is abundant and loyal to you.
Cuts both ways — scale deters entrants, but the same dominance invites caps and antitrust.

origin.who: Bank of America (BankAmericard) and the banks behind Interbank / Master Charge
origin.what_problem_forced_it: A single bank's card was only useful at merchants that bank had signed. Merchants and banks needed a universal system so ANY bank's card would work at ANY merchant — the network was the shared switchboard that made cards interoperable, and the toll paid for running it.

operator.name: Dee Hock, founder of Visa
operator.what_they_did: Reorganized BankAmericard into a member-owned cooperative (Visa) in the 1970s — a deliberately decentralized structure owned by the banks that used it, so competitors could cooperate on shared rails while competing for cardholders.
operator.outcome: Visa grew into the largest payment network on earth; the cooperative later went public as a for-profit company worth hundreds of billions.

counterexample.name: The Durbin Amendment (2010) and interchange litigation
counterexample.what_they_did: US regulators capped debit-card interchange, and a long-running antitrust fight forced credit interchange concessions and settlements into the 2020s.
counterexample.why_it_broke: The model's dependence on interchange is also its exposure: when the fee that aligns banks is capped by law, the flywheel's fuel is rationed — proof that a regulatory moat can become a regulatory ceiling.

numbers.label: Visa+MC share of US credit volume

unknowns: Exact split of the network's own take between assessment, data-processing, and cross-border fees is not broken out here.
Figures come from secondary sources citing company filings, not read directly from the 10-Ks in this entry.
Interchange rates and settlement terms are actively changing through ongoing litigation — treat 2025 figures as a moving target.
Non-US economics differ sharply (e.g. EU interchange is capped far lower) — these numbers skew US.

recall.glyph_prompt: A tollbooth straddling a massive highway of money. Trillions of cars stream through and the network clips a single coin off each one — without ever owning a car. The fat toll doesn't stay in the booth: it's handed to the banks that sent the drivers, so the banks keep sending more.
three_questions: On a $100 swipe, who actually keeps most of the ~$2–3 fee — the network or the bank? (the bank, via interchange; the network keeps a thin assessment)
Why do issuing banks want to hand out Visa/Mastercard cards specifically?
What is the network's real moat, and what two forces threaten it? (two-sided network effect; interchange regulation and real-time/stablecoin rails)

scale.metric: combined annual net revenue of the two largest networks
